relationship: Multidimensional integration is the operation underlying the posterior predictive (§6.1) and the marginal likelihood (§2.4). The §10 Bayes factor is a ratio of multivariate integrals; the §11 grid quadrature is the 1-D version we can compute when the integral has no closed form.

Bayes' theorem in §2.2 is conditional probability applied to parameter spaces — the posterior P(θ | data) is the conditional density of the parameter given the observation. The continuous version operates on densities; the discrete version on probabilities. Both rest on the conditional-probability definition developed there.

The continuous form of Bayes' theorem (§2.2) operates on probability density functions, not probability masses. Readers need the density-vs-mass distinction — and the change-of-variables story for densities — to follow the prior, likelihood, and posterior as densities over θ.

The Binomial likelihood for the A/B-test running example (§1.2) is the data-generating distribution. Beta–Binomial conjugacy, Gamma–Poisson conjugacy, and the Dirichlet–Multinomial generalization in §4.4 all rest on the discrete-distribution catalog developed there.

The exponential-family construction (§4.5) explains why the conjugate-prior catalog of §4.4 exists at all. Every conjugate pair we name — Beta–Binomial, Gamma–Poisson, Normal–Normal, Dirichlet–Multinomial, Normal-Inverse-Gamma — is an instance of the generic exponential-family conjugate-prior construction; this prerequisite is the structural reason.

Sufficient statistics characterize which features of the data the posterior depends on — and underwrite the §8.1 order-invariance and sequential-updating results. The stopping-rule irrelevance in §8.2 also depends on the factorization argument that sufficiency makes precise.
The Hessian of the negative log-posterior in §3.1 is a Jacobian computation against the gradient; KFAC and diagonal-Fisher reductions in §3.4 are structured approximations to this Jacobian.

BNN posteriors are MVN near the MAP estimate by Bernstein–von Mises (§25.8 Thm 5); the Laplace approximation (§25.8 Rem 16) is the canonical construction lifted from formalstatistics into deep-learning scale in §3 of this topic.

Bernstein–von Mises is the Bayesian CLT — the posterior of √n(θ − θ_MLE) converges in total variation to N(0, I(θ_0)^{-1}). §2.3 cites this theorem as the asymptotic justification for the Laplace approximation in well-specified BNNs.

Bernstein–von Mises convergence is in total variation distance, hence in distribution. §2.3 invokes the total-variation framing to argue that in the large-data limit, the BNN posterior is approximated arbitrarily well by a single Gaussian centered at the MLE.

Weight priors w ~ N_p(0, σ²I) are multivariate Normal. The Laplace approximation in §3 produces a Gaussian posterior whose inverse covariance is the Hessian of the negative log-posterior at the MAP. §4 and §6 each carry MVN-sampling subroutines.

Hierarchical priors over groups of weights (e.g., one variance per layer) and the partial-pooling-via-shrinkage view inform §3.3's discussion of structured prior choices and §8.5's cold-posterior remark on prior misspecification.

Bayesian posteriors require $\int \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior}\, d\theta$ over unbounded parameter spaces. Conjugate priors (Gamma–Poisson, Beta–Binomial, Normal–Normal) are designed so these improper integrals reduce to ratios of Gamma and Beta functions, yielding closed-form posteriors used throughout the nonparametric machinery.

Multi-parameter posteriors require integrating over high-dimensional parameter spaces; Fubini enables the conditional decompositions that underwrite Gibbs sampling, and Monte Carlo methods estimate the intractable marginals. For nonparametric models, the parameter is itself a measure, and Fubini-style decompositions extend to product probability spaces.

Posterior computation requires integrating likelihood × prior over the parameter space. When conjugacy is unavailable, numerical quadrature (trapezoidal, Simpson, Gaussian) provides the computational backbone, and the integration-error bounds from the formalcalculus topic inform how much approximation error these quadratures introduce.

The Dirichlet process, Chinese-restaurant process, hierarchical Dirichlet process, and stick-breaking construction generalize the hierarchical-Bayes-with-partial-pooling story to nonparametric mixture models. Where finite-Bayes pools toward a hyperprior, nonparametrics pools toward a random base measure — the structural inheritance is direct, and §28.10 Rem 25 on the formalstatistics side explicitly forward-points to this topic.

The Taylor expansion of the AIPW score around the true nuisances underlies the §6.3 product-of-errors decomposition and the §8.2 Neyman-orthogonality derivation. The mean-value-theorem-based argument that the bias has a second-order remainder in the nuisance estimation error is what licenses ML nuisances in the DML framework.

The §9 instrumental-variables identification argument relies on the implicit-function theorem to ensure the first-stage map $e(Z) \to D$ is locally invertible when the relevance condition $\operatorname{Cov}(Z, D) \neq 0$ holds. The rank condition for IV identification is an inverse/implicit-function existence claim at the population level.

The §3.4 g-formula functional $\mathbb{E}_X[\mu_1(X) - \mu_0(X)] = \int (\mu_1(x) - \mu_0(x)) \, dF_X(x)$ is an explicit multivariate integral over the covariate distribution. The longitudinal extension in §14.2 iterates this integral across time-points, requiring the Fubini machinery developed in the formalcalculus multiple-integrals topic.

The §6 AIPW estimator's efficient-influence-function representation, the §7 TMLE rate theorem, and the §8 DML $\sqrt{n}$ result all depend on uniform central-limit theorems and Donsker-class machinery developed in the empirical-processes topic. The functional delta method underwrites the semiparametric asymptotic theory throughout §§4–8.

Logistic regression is the canonical propensity-score model throughout §§4–8, and GLM machinery (M-estimation, sandwich variance, score equations) underlies the §4.3 asymptotic-normality result for IPW. The outcome regression in §5 is a generic GLM-style fit, with the partial-linear Robinson model that threads the §13 worked example a GLM with semiparametric component.

The §5 outcome regression, the §9 two-stage least squares framework, and the partial-linear Robinson (1988) model that threads the worked example all build directly on linear-regression machinery. The §8 DML cross-fitting reference is Chernozhukov et al. (2018), which generalizes the linear-regression sandwich variance to ML-nuisance settings.

AIPW (§6), TMLE (§7), and DML (§8) are M-estimators / Z-estimators with augmented score functions, and their asymptotic-normality follows from the same Stefanski–Boos (2002) M-estimator framework developed in the point-estimation topic. The §4.3 sandwich variance and the §6.4 EIF-based variance are both M-estimator sandwich formulas.

Wald confidence intervals for the ATE — appearing throughout §§4, 6, 8, 13 — invoke the duality between hypothesis tests and CIs developed in the confidence-intervals-and-duality topic. The §12 Rosenbaum bounds and Anderson–Rubin confidence sets for IV (§9.4) are non-Wald CIs constructed via test inversion using the same duality.

The §9.4 weak-IV-robust tests (Anderson–Rubin, conditional likelihood ratio) and the §12 Rosenbaum sensitivity bounds are inverted from hypothesis tests of the null treatment effect under various nuisance assumptions. The §11.4 heterogeneity tests for CATE are hypothesis tests of constant treatment effect.

The mean-shift derivation in §3 uses the chain rule and gradient computation in $\mathbb{R}^d$; §4's convergence proof uses the multivariate Taylor expansion around a mode. formalcalculus's gradient topic supplies the partial-derivative / chain-rule machinery readers might want to review if rusty.

Topic 30's KDE estimator $\hat f_h$ is the substrate on which mean-shift performs gradient ascent (§§2–3). §30.3's Nadaraya–Watson construction is the closest sister to mean-shift's sample-weighted-mean form, and the bandwidth-bias-variance trade-off in §30.5 is the prerequisite framing for §5's bandwidth-mode-count duality. The multivariate-Gaussian-kernel substrate (§6.1) and the Mahalanobis-distance reading of GMM responsibilities (§10.2) require the multivariate-normal machinery — covariance matrices, density form, marginal/conditional rules — that formalstatistics develops in its multivariate-distributions topic.

Tail bounds $P(X > t) = \int_t^\infty f(x)\,dx$ are improper integrals. The decay rate (exponential vs. polynomial) determines sub-Gaussian vs. heavy-tailed behavior, and Stirling's approximation appears in sharp bounds for binomial tails via the entropy method.

Concentration inequalities quantify convergence rates for sequences of random variables — how fast empirical averages converge to their expectations. The $\varepsilon$–$N$ framework is what makes 'with probability $1 - \delta$, the deviation is at most $\varepsilon$' a meaningful sequence-convergence statement at finite $n$.

Chernoff bounds produce geometric series in tail probabilities, and the ratio test applied to moment-generating-function expansions determines the strength of exponential concentration. Series-convergence theory is what lets us interchange limit and sum in the MGF analysis underpinning sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential classes.

Markov, Chebyshev, and Hoeffding bounds are all bounds on the measure of tail sets $P(|X - \mu| > t)$. The $\sigma$-algebra framework gives the formal machinery for assigning probability to such tail events, and the monotone-class theorem is the technical hammer behind extending bounds from simple events to arbitrary measurable ones.

Uniform-convergence bounds like Glivenko–Cantelli and the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality are concentration inequalities applied uniformly over function classes. The DKW inequality bounds $\|\hat F_n - F\|_\infty$ — the sup-norm distance between empirical and true CDFs — at rate $O(1/\sqrt n)$.

Topic 29 §29.7's distribution-free CI for the population quantile $\xi_p$ via paired order statistics relies on the same exchangeability + rank-symmetry argument that drives Theorem 1 here; conformal prediction extends rank symmetry from a fixed parameter to a random variable. §29.10 Rem 21 explicitly motivates Vovk-Gammerman-Shafer's distribution-free prediction as that generalization.

Topic 32's uniform-convergence theory (DKW inequality, VC dimension, Glivenko-Cantelli) is the asymptotic alternative to conformal's exact finite-sample coverage. The two routes meet at distribution-free prediction: empirical-processes pays a uniform-convergence rate; conformal pays only marginal validity. §1 here frames the trade-off.

The Weierstrass extreme-value theorem — continuous functions on compact sets attain their extrema — is the foundational existence result for convex optimization. Compactness of sublevel sets for coercive convex functions guarantees minimizers exist even on unbounded domains, the prerequisite for every subsequent convergence argument.

Convex functions on open sets are automatically continuous — a non-trivial theorem proved by the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ machinery. Lower-semicontinuity generalizes continuity for optimization, and the Lipschitz-gradient condition ($\nabla f$ is $L$-Lipschitz) is the key smoothness assumption every convergence proof in the optimization track relies on.

For convex functions, the gradient provides a global lower bound: $f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top(y - x)$. This first-order convexity condition is the foundation of convex optimization — the gradient at any point gives a tangent hyperplane that lies entirely below the graph.

A $C^2$ function is convex iff $H_f(x) \succeq 0$ for all $x$. Strong convexity ($H_f \succeq \mu I$) gives the convergence rate $\mu/L$ for gradient descent, where $L$ is the Lipschitz constant of the gradient (equivalently, the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian when bounded).

A twice-differentiable function is convex iff its first-order Taylor expansion is a global lower bound: $f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top(y - x)$. This characterization follows directly from Taylor's theorem with non-negative second derivative — the bridge between convex analysis and the calculus framework.

The §2.2 detour on absolute continuity uses the Radon–Nikodym theorem to ground the density-ratio function $r = \mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}q$ as a measurable object before the importance-weighting identity is applied; without it, the proof in Move 2 of §2.2 would be merely formal manipulation of $p/q$ on the set where the pointwise expression is undefined.

DRE generalizes the plug-in KDE-divided-by-KDE estimator from KDE, replacing it with direct estimation that avoids the §1.1 tail-blowup pathology; KDE bandwidth selection, kernel choice, and the AMISE rate machinery transfer to KMM (§4), KLIEP (§5), and uLSIF (§6) verbatim.

KLIEP's KL-divergence framing in §5.1 is built on MLE machinery — the constrained-MLE Lagrangian, the consistency theorem under misspecification, and the projected-gradient algorithm all reuse standard MLE technology applied to a ratio model rather than a density model.

The Marchenko–Pastur measure introduced in §5 is a probability measure on the nonnegative reals, and the §5.2 Stieltjes-transform derivation integrates 1/(λ−z) against the MP density. Comfort with Lebesgue integration on the line (and limiting arguments through the Stieltjes inversion formula) is the substrate for the §6 closed-form bias-variance integrals.

Provides the OLS substrate the entire topic builds on — normal equations, projection geometry, the bias-variance decomposition, and the condition-number diagnostics. The classical U-curve picture in §2.1 is read off this topic's parametric variance formula σ²(k+1)/n. §6's overparameterized revision uses the same decomposition with bias and variance components governed by Marchenko–Pastur integrals.

Discharges the forward-pointer this topic declares. §4's RidgelessVsRidge contrast is the explicit answer to 'what does ridge do in the overparameterized regime?' — the SVD shrinkage factor s/(s²+λ) smooths the threshold spike, and the λ → 0 limit is the ridgeless minimum-norm interpolator that the rest of §§4–9 analyzes. The reciprocal `formalmlConnections: double-descent` is already declared on the formalstatistics side.

The weak-convergence framework that all of §§2–3 lean on lives there: convergence-in-distribution as weak convergence of probability measures, the Portmanteau theorem (used explicitly in the Khintchine / type-convergence proof of §2.3), and Slutsky's theorem (used implicitly in the same proof and throughout §3).

The Donsker / functional-CLT machinery in Topic 32 is the framework for 'what happens to the entire empirical CDF as n grows.' EVT is the analog at the tail rather than the bulk. The technical machinery overlaps directly in the slow-variation arguments of §3 and the regular-variation expansions of §5. Topic 32's outgoing edge to extreme-value-theory is already declared as a deferred reciprocal in the audit dump; this entry resolves it.

The sample maximum $M_n = X_{(n)}$ is the extreme order statistic; Topic 29 treats the joint distribution of order statistics and the asymptotic theory of $X_{(\lceil pn \rceil)}$ for fixed $p \in (0, 1)$. EVT continues this story for $p \to 1$ (the maximum, §§1–4) and $p$ close to 1 (high quantiles via §5 POT).

The §2.4 Karhunen-Loève expansion expresses a centered GP as an L^2-convergent series of independent Gaussians; the §5.1 marginal-likelihood derivation invokes Gaussian–Gaussian convolution, a Lebesgue-integral identity at base.
GPs are infinite-dimensional multivariate Normals; §3.2's conditioning lemma and §5.1's marginal-likelihood derivation both reduce to multivariate-Normal density and conjugacy work that lives there.

The univariate-Gaussian density and Gaussian–Gaussian convolution identity are invoked throughout §3 (predictive marginals at single test inputs) and §5.1 (the marginal-likelihood derivation collapses two independent Gaussians into one).
The §1 parametric Bayesian regression starting point is the conjugate-Gaussian update from prior-selection; §5.2's Bayesian Occam's razor is one instance of the model-evidence framework.

GPs are stochastic processes defined by their finite-dimensional joints; §2.2's Kolmogorov-consistency proof bridges from those joints to a probability measure on path space via the extension theorem.

Rigorous foundation for the risk functional R(h) = ∫ ℓ(h(x), y) dP(x, y) as a Lebesgue integral against the population probability measure. The gap between empirical averages (Riemann-style sample sums) and population integrals (Lebesgue integrals) is the central object of every bound in this topic; the change-of-variables and dominated-convergence machinery developed in lebesgue-integral underwrites every convergence claim here.

Sister-site source of uniform-convergence machinery — Glivenko–Cantelli, Donsker classes, and the bracketing / metric-entropy framework that §8's real-valued function-class material specializes. Topic 32 §32.4's G-C-for-VC bound is the empirical-process core of the canonical Rademacher bound developed in §7.

The pointwise concentration in §2 is the WLLN with an explicit rate: for any fixed h, P(|R̂_n(h) − R(h)| > ε) ≤ δ. §3's finite-class bound and §4's Glivenko–Cantelli theorem extend the WLLN from a single hypothesis to uniform statements across an entire hypothesis class — the conceptual move that defines learning theory.

Uniform convergence (Definition 4) — a.s. convergence of sup_h |R̂_S(h) − R(h)| → 0 — is the right mode of convergence for the §§4–7 development. The §4 Glivenko–Cantelli theorem is uniform-a.s. convergence; the §6 symmetrization argument lifts pointwise mean-square convergence to uniform expectation control via Jensen's inequality.

Rademacher symmetrization (§6) routes the generalization-gap statistic through a sum of bounded mean-zero random variables — the CLT regime. The empirical Rademacher complexity itself converges to its population expectation at the CLT rate O(1/√n), giving the §7 canonical O(1/√n) generalization bound for bounded loss classes.

Hoeffding's inequality (§3) and McDiarmid's bounded-differences inequality (§7) are large-deviation statements: the empirical risk concentrates around the true risk at an exponential rate. The §3 union bound and the §7 two-step concentration both use these large-deviation rates directly, and the §11 algorithmic-stability bound applies McDiarmid to a different bounded-differences functional.

Universal-approximation theorems for neural networks (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991, Barron) are the function-class results that justify gradient descent on neural objectives at all — without dense, well-approximated function classes there is nothing to optimize over. Barron's $O(1/\sqrt n)$ rate is the same one Bernstein polynomials achieve, built in the Stone–Weierstrass framework of the formalcalculus topic.

Operator norms $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ bound the Lipschitz constants of linear gradient maps and feed directly into spectral-normalization techniques that stabilize gradient flow through deep networks. The open-mapping theorem provides the bounded-inverse guarantees behind invertible-layer analysis.

Gradient descent is the discrete-time shadow of the continuous gradient flow $\dot\theta = -\nabla L(\theta)$, a variational object whose trajectories are stationary points of an action functional. The direct method underwrites existence of minimizers in the function-space settings (gradient descent in Sobolev spaces, infinite-width network limits) referenced in §6.

The reparameterization trick $z = \mu + \sigma\varepsilon$ for variational objectives moves parameters outside the expectation by a smooth change of variables, enabling unbiased gradient estimates through sampling. Mirror descent's iterate map $x \mapsto \nabla\varphi(x)$ is itself a diffeomorphism — Euclidean descent becomes Bregman descent under this substitution.

Existence of minimizers for regularized objectives $f + \lambda\|\cdot\|^2$ rides on coercivity plus lower-semicontinuity to extract a convergent subsequence by Bolzano–Weierstrass. The extreme-value theorem on compact sublevel sets is the existence result our convergence proofs assume in the background.

Single-variable gradient descent $\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta f'(\theta_t)$ is the prototype we generalize to $\mathbb{R}^d$. The chain rule from that topic is the engine of backpropagation through layered networks — every gradient we compute is a recursive chain-rule application down a computation graph.

$L$-Lipschitz continuity of the gradient $\|
abla f(x) - 
abla f(y)\| \le L\|x - y\|$ is the uniform-continuity statement that controls step-size requirements ($\eta < 2/L$ for vanilla GD on $L$-smooth functions). Without uniform continuity of $
abla f$, no convergence guarantee in this topic survives.

Gradient descent is the explicit Euler discretization of the first-order ODE $\dot\theta = -\nabla L(\theta)$. Picard–Lindelöf gives existence and uniqueness of the continuous flow when $\nabla L$ is Lipschitz — exactly the smoothness assumption underwriting every convergence rate in §3. The learning rate $\eta$ is the Euler step size; smaller $\eta$ tracks the continuous flow more faithfully.

Random Fourier features turn shift-invariant kernel methods into explicit feature-space gradient descent via Monte Carlo integration over the spectral measure. The Fourier-analytic perspective also enters the neural-tangent-kernel limit, where gradient descent on wide networks becomes kernel regression with the NTK as its kernel.

The gradient $
abla f$ is the steepest-ascent direction; $-
abla f$ is what we step along. Orthogonality of $
abla f$ to level sets is the geometric reason gradient descent cuts across contour lines, and the directional-derivative inequality $D_u f \le \|
abla f\|$ is why no other direction beats steepest descent locally.

Second-order methods (Newton, quasi-Newton, L-BFGS) precondition by $H^{-1}$, replacing gradient steps with curvature-corrected steps. The Hessian's eigenvalues set the condition number $\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ that drives our linear-convergence rate; diagonal-Hessian approximations sit implicitly inside Adam and RMSProp.

Proximal operators are orthogonal projections in Hilbert spaces, and the Riesz representation lets us identify gradients with descent directions in dual coordinates. Gradient descent in RKHS — the formulation underlying kernel-method optimization — is exactly this geometric picture made functional.

The inverse-function theorem licenses local invertibility of the gradient map $\nabla L$ near non-degenerate minima where the Hessian is non-singular, so small perturbations from optimum produce proportional gradient signals. This is the local-convergence story behind Newton-type methods and the basin-of-attraction analysis in §4.

Backpropagation is the multivariate chain rule realized as a product of layer Jacobians, evaluated right-to-left via vector–Jacobian products. Reverse-mode AD computes $\nabla L$ in one backward sweep regardless of parameter count — the asymmetry between forward and reverse mode is a Jacobian-product associativity argument.

The interchange $\nabla\mathbb{E}[L(\theta, X)] = \mathbb{E}[\nabla L(\theta, X)]$ that licenses stochastic-gradient unbiasedness is a dominated-convergence theorem application — the single most important ML use of Lebesgue integration. All of §5's SGD analysis quietly leans on it.

Gradient flow $\theta(t)$ traces a curve in parameter space, and the gradient theorem yields $L(\theta(T)) - L(\theta(0)) = -\int_0^T \|\nabla L\|^2\,dt \le 0$ — the path-integral identity proving monotonic loss decrease along the continuous flow that discrete GD discretizes.

On a quadratic $L(\theta) = \tfrac12 \theta^\top H\theta$, gradient descent is the linear system $\dot\theta = -H\theta$ with solution $\theta(t) = e^{-Ht}\theta_0$. Each eigencomponent decays as $e^{-\lambda_i t}$; the condition number $\kappa(H)$ is the ratio of fastest to slowest decay and pinpoints why ill-conditioned objectives converge slowly.

The descent lemma $f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top(y - x) + (L/2)\|y - x\|^2$ — the cornerstone of every $L$-smooth convergence proof in §3 — is a direct corollary of second-order Taylor expansion with Lipschitz-gradient remainder bound. Newton's method replaces the quadratic upper bound with the true quadratic Taylor model and pays linear→quadratic convergence for it.

The contraction-mapping theorem gives convergence of fixed-point iterations, the prototype Banach analysis we lift to the gradient-descent map $T(\theta) = \theta - \eta\nabla L(\theta)$. Lipschitz continuity of $T$, controlled by $L$-smoothness of $L$, supplies the contraction constant $\le 1 - \eta\mu$ on $\mu$-strongly-convex objectives — exactly the linear rate in §3.2.

The expected risk $\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}[\ell(\theta; x, y)]$ is a multivariate integral over the joint data distribution. Each SGD mini-batch is a Monte Carlo estimate of this integral; the variance of the estimate is what §5's SGD convergence analysis tracks as the noise floor of stochastic-gradient descent.

Second-order Taylor expansion $T_2(y) = f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top(y - x) + \tfrac12 (y - x)^\top H(y - x)$ is the quadratic local model Newton's method uses directly and that we bound via Lipschitz gradient in the descent lemma. Quadratic convergence near the optimum is the rate when $T_2$ is exact (the quadratic-objective case).

The iterates $\{\theta_t\}$ form a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Convergence — whether to a stationary point, a minimum, or along a saddle's stable manifold — and convergence rates ($O(1/k)$, linear, quadratic) are statements about this sequence using exactly the $\varepsilon$–$N$ machinery developed in formalcalculus.

The Robbins–Monro step-size conditions for SGD — $\sum_t \alpha_t = \infty$ and $\sum_t \alpha_t^2 < \infty$ — are series-convergence statements. The $p$-series test classifies polynomial-decay schedules $\alpha_t = c/t^p$: both conditions hold iff $p \in (\tfrac12, 1]$, the canonical SGD-rate window.

The Lee–Simchowitz–Jordan–Recht (2016) result that gradient descent avoids strict saddles almost surely is a measure-theoretic statement: the stable manifold of any strict saddle has Lebesgue measure zero in initialization space, so generic initialization escapes saddles with probability one.

Convergence of gradient descent to a local minimum is asymptotic stability of the gradient-flow ODE $\dot\theta = -\nabla L(\theta)$. The Hessian's eigenvalues at a critical point determine the dynamics: positive eigenvalues are stable directions (convergence), negative are unstable (escape along a saddle's unstable manifold).

The divergence theorem reads the geometry of gradient flow off $\nabla \cdot (-\nabla L) = -\Delta L$: regions of positive Laplacian have trajectories diverging from the local mean, negative Laplacian focuses them inward — connecting loss-surface curvature to the convergence geometry of optimization.

The mini-batch gradient is an average of $B$ iid gradient samples; by the CLT, its fluctuations around the true gradient are Gaussian at scale $\sigma/\sqrt B$. This motivates the learning-rate schedule $\eta \propto 1/\sqrt t$ and explains why larger batches reduce noise with diminishing returns.

Sub-Gaussian gradient-noise analysis justifies SGD step-size schedules. Azuma–Hoeffding applies to the martingale formed by cumulative SGD gradient errors, giving non-asymptotic convergence rates that the large-deviations topic supplies as concentration substrate.

SGD convergence under Robbins–Monro conditions ($\sum \alpha_t = \infty$, $\sum \alpha_t^2 < \infty$) is proved via the SLLN and martingale convergence. Polyak averaging — computing the running mean of SGD iterates — converges almost surely to the optimum by the SLLN.

SGD convergence analysis is an exercise in modes of convergence. With decreasing step sizes satisfying the Robbins–Monro conditions, the iterates converge almost surely to a local minimum; with constant step size, convergence is only in probability to a neighborhood. Both regimes use the mode-hierarchy and Slutsky-style combination rules from the formalstatistics modes-of-convergence topic.

The mini-batch gradient is a biased estimator of the full gradient (if the batch is a strict subset); its variance is $\sigma^2/B$ for batch size $B$. The learning-rate schedule navigates the bias-variance tradeoff in optimization, with the point-estimation framework supplying the bias/MSE/efficiency vocabulary.

KKT subgradient calculus, soft-thresholding derivation from convex optimality conditions, Lagrangian duality between penalized and constrained forms, ISTA / FISTA convergence analysis via the descent lemma and Lyapunov-function arguments. The §3 FISTA convergence proof leans heavily on the descent lemma and the proximal-gradient inequality from this foundation topic.

The high-dimensional probability / concentration substrate — sub-Gaussian tail bounds, union-bound deviation inequalities, multivariate-integration moves used in the lasso oracle inequality's deviation step (§5.5) for controlling $\|\mathbf{X}^\top \boldsymbol\varepsilon / n\|_\infty$. Same use as in kernel-regression's §3.3 Taylor-with-remainder bias derivation.

Least-squares regression and its penalized variants (ridge, lasso, elastic net) minimize $\|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2$ — an $L^2$ norm — with closed-form existence via $L^2$ projection onto a closed subspace. The §10 debiased-lasso analysis leans on $L^2(P_X)$-norm convergence rates throughout; the $L^p$ machinery built in lp-spaces §§3–7 is what makes those rate statements precise.

Conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]$ is the best $L^2$ predictor — the Radon–Nikodym derivative of a restricted measure — and least-squares regression computes it in $\mathbb{R}^n$. In the $p \gg n$ regime, the debiased-lasso $\sqrt n$-consistency proof uses absolute-continuity hypotheses to keep the conditional-density manipulations rigorous.

Covers ridge / lasso / elastic net at the standard $n > p$ regime — KKT subgradient, soft-thresholding for orthogonal designs, coordinate-descent solvers, cross-validated $\lambda$ selection. This ML topic extends the parametric lasso to the $p \gg n$ regime where standard inference breaks down, adds the oracle inequality + restricted-eigenvalue / irrepresentable conditions, and adds debiased-lasso inference.

OLS, normal equations, geometric picture of projection onto column space — same prerequisite used by kernel-regression and local-regression. Reference for the §1 "OLS overfits when $p > n$" geometric hook and for the §10 OLS-baseline confidence-interval comparison.

The inferential apparatus — Type I / Type II errors, confidence intervals, p-values, Wald and likelihood-ratio tests under normal asymptotics. The §10 debiased lasso produces a $\sqrt n$-consistent normal estimator; the resulting CI / hypothesis test is the formalstatistics testing-theory framework applied to a high-dimensional setting, with the PoSI undercoverage demonstration and debiased-lasso fix appealing directly to the standard testing framework.

When $p \gg n$ the GLM design matrix is rank-deficient and ordinary IRLS fails — exactly the regime this topic operates in. §22.10 Rem 28 of the formalstatistics GLM topic forward-points to the high-dimensional treatment via penalized GLMs (the regularization-and-penalized-estimation topic is the bridge), and the minimax-rate / double-descent stories then live here in the ML-track treatment.

When $p \gg n$, likelihood-based information criteria degenerate — the model-comparison story this topic answers. Extended BIC (Chen–Chen 2008), stability selection (Meinshausen–Bühlmann 2010), and knockoffs (Barber–Candès 2015) are the high-dimensional extensions of the classical AIC/BIC framework, and §24.10 Rem 25 of the formalstatistics topic forward-points to exactly the treatment here.

Geodesics on the statistical manifold are calculus-of-variations problems with the Fisher-Rao length functional as the action. The Euler–Lagrange equation governs the natural-gradient flow, and dually flat structures on exponential families correspond to convex-conjugate variational principles.

The Fisher information matrix transforms under reparametrization $\tilde\theta = \phi(\theta)$ via $\tilde I(\tilde\theta) = J^\top I(\theta) J$ — a Jacobian sandwich. Reparametrization invariance of natural gradient descent is exactly this covariance property, lifted from the change-of-variables formula for densities.

Score functions in exponential families decompose into orthogonal components under the Fisher inner product, and the orthogonal-projection structure of Fourier analysis carries over to the geometry of statistical manifolds — the natural gradient projects onto the tangent space defined by the score basis.

The Fisher information matrix $I(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[-\nabla^2 \log p(x | \theta)]$ is the expected Hessian of the negative log-likelihood under regularity conditions. The natural gradient $I^{-1}(\theta)\nabla L$ is Newton's method adapted to the Riemannian geometry of the model — curvature here is the Hessian of the KL divergence at the parameter.

The statistical manifold of a parametric family is locally diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^d$ via the inverse-function theorem whenever the Fisher information matrix is non-singular. Reparametrization invariance — and the well-definedness of coordinate changes on the parameter space — relies on this local-invertibility guarantee.

The Jacobian sandwich $I(\phi(\eta)) = J_\phi^\top I(\eta) J_\phi$ expresses how the natural Riemannian metric on a statistical manifold transforms under coordinate changes. Every parameter-invariant computation in this topic — natural gradient, Cramér–Rao bound, Amari α-connections — uses this transformation law.

KL divergence $D_\mathrm{KL}(P \| Q) = \int \log(dP/dQ)\, dP$ and cross-entropy are Lebesgue integrals against probability measures. Their properties — non-negativity by Jensen, convexity, additivity over independent factors — all follow from integral inequalities developed in the formalcalculus topic.

Geodesics on the statistical manifold minimize the Fisher-Rao length functional — a line integral of the metric tensor along a curve in parameter space. Path length in the Fisher-Rao metric is the geodesic notion of statistical distinguishability, and natural-gradient trajectories track these geodesics in the small-step limit.

The Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$ is the Hessian of the KL divergence at $\theta = \theta_0$, computed by second-order Taylor expansion of $D_\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \| p_{\theta_0})$. The resulting Riemannian metric on parameter space is the geometric foundation of every natural-gradient method.

KL divergence $D_\mathrm{KL}(P \| Q) = \mathbb{E}_P[\log(dP/dQ)]$ is the expected log-Radon–Nikodym derivative — the most basic information-geometric divergence is literally a change of measure. Fisher information is the variance of the score, which is $\nabla \log(dP/d\lambda)$ for a fixed reference measure $\lambda$.

Natural-gradient-descent stability hinges on the eigenvalues of the preconditioned Hessian $F^{-1}\nabla^2 L$, where the Fisher metric reshapes the convergence landscape. The dually flat structure on exponential families gives a Lyapunov-stable flow with the KL divergence as a natural Lyapunov function.

The Fisher-Rao volume form $\sqrt{\det I(\theta)}\,d\theta$ on the statistical manifold induces surface integrals that measure 'statistical area' — Jeffreys' prior is the normalized version of this volume form. The divergence theorem on the manifold connects natural-gradient-flow conservation to boundary flux.

The Fisher information $I(\eta) = A''(\eta)$ for a canonical exponential family is the second derivative of the log-partition function — a closed-form construction of the Riemannian metric on parameter space. The natural/expectation duality of exponential families is the prototypical dually flat structure that Amari's α-connections generalize.

Fisher information is defined via the score function $\partial_\theta \log f(x; \theta)$, which requires the PDF parametrization that this formalstatistics topic builds. The statistical manifold is the space of distributions on a fixed sample space, and tangent vectors at a distribution are score-class equivalence classes of random variables.

The bias-variance asymptotics in §3-§4 integrate the kernel against the design density f_X(x) dx on the support of X. The change-of-variables substitution u = (z-x)/h used throughout §3.2 and the d-dimensional volume scaling h^d in §6.3 are standard multivariate-integration moves; the §6.1 product kernel R(K) = R(K_1)^d uses Fubini.

The §3.2 second-order Taylor expansion of f_X(x+hu) and g(x+hu) = m(x+hu)f_X(x+hu) around x, with explicit h² remainder term, is the load-bearing technical move of the entire bias derivation. The §6.3 multivariate version uses the same expansion with the Hessian ∇²m replacing the second derivative. §8.2's local-linear bias also leans on Taylor.

The §3 bias and §4 variance derivations are direct lifts of the kernel-density-estimation machinery applied to the conditional-mean ratio m̂_h(x) = r̂(x)/f̂_X(x). Same kernel moment conditions (∫K = 1, ∫uK = 0, ∫u²K = μ_2), same h² bias / 1/(nh) variance rates, and the Silverman bandwidth heuristic in §5.1 is the kernel-density-estimation rule applied directly.

The §2.3 reframing of NW as degree-zero local polynomial regression draws directly on weighted-least-squares theory from linear regression. The §8.2 local-linear extension is locally-weighted OLS with two parameters (intercept + slope); its WLS solution generalizes the single-coefficient form via the kernel-weighted normal equations.

The Euler–Lagrange equation is the infinite-dimensional prototype for first-order optimality conditions, and Lagrangian duality generalizes the constrained variational problems of formalcalculus to the convex-optimization setting we work in here. KKT conditions are the discrete counterpart of the Euler–Lagrange / transversality system, and saddle-point characterizations of strong duality match the variational stationarity in the calculus topic.

Multivariate-integration substrate for the §4 bias-variance computations and the §8 multivariate full-degree expansion. The change-of-variables u = (z-x)/h that converts the kernel-weighted moments into kernel-moment integrals, and the boundary-truncated form mu_j^(c) = integral over [-c, infty), are standard multivariate-integration moves used throughout the bias derivations.

Taylor expansion to order p+1 is the load-bearing technical move of the §4 bias derivation at general degree p — higher-order than the order-2 expansion that kernel-regression's NW analysis uses. The §4.1 residual-decomposition argument uses the column-space projection identity to absorb the first p+1 Taylor terms, leaving only the (p+1)-st derivative remainder to drive the bias.

Locally-weighted least squares with a degree-p polynomial design matrix is this topic's central machinery. The (X^T W X)^{-1} X^T W y normal equations are the linear-regression formulas applied at every evaluation point with location-adaptive design and weight matrices; the §3 equivalent-kernel formulation is the classical projection-onto-column-space picture from linear regression read in kernel-weighted units.

Kernel families and bandwidth-moment conditions mu_2(K), R(K) port directly from KDE — same K, same h, same kernel constants. The bandwidth-selection methods (Silverman, plug-in, LOO-CV, GCV) transfer to local polynomial regression via the same linear-smoother machinery; the §3.3 moment-matching identities are the local-polynomial analog of KDE's higher-order kernels.

The density-transformation formula $p_X(x) = p_Z(\phi^{-1}(x))\,|\det J_{\phi^{-1}}(x)|$ is the probabilistic form of the change-of-variables theorem. Pushforward measures under measurable maps are this theorem at the level of $\sigma$-algebras; absolute continuity of the pushforward is preserved precisely when the Jacobian determinant is well-defined.

Tightness of probability measures (Prokhorov's theorem) is a compactness condition: a family is tight if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists a compact $K$ with $\mu(K) > 1 - \varepsilon$ for every $\mu$ in the family. Weak-convergence proofs invoke this every time they pass from a tight sequence to a convergent subsequence.

Stochastic differential equations $dX_t = f(X_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t$ extend deterministic ODEs by adding Brownian noise. Itô's existence-and-uniqueness theorem is the stochastic analog of Picard–Lindelöf, using the same Lipschitz condition and contraction argument lifted to a space of stochastic processes.

Every probability density satisfies $\int f(x)\,dx = 1$, an improper integral over $\mathbb{R}$. The Gamma and Beta functions are normalizing constants for Gamma, Chi-squared, Beta, and Dirichlet distributions; the transition from improper Riemann to Lebesgue integration is exactly the step that makes measure-theoretic probability rigorous.

Joint densities and marginals are computed via Fubini's theorem, and every two-variable probabilistic computation is a multiple integral. The Fubini–Tonelli theorem generalizes this to Lebesgue integrals on $\sigma$-finite measure spaces — the technical underpinning of conditional-expectation manipulations.

The Riemann integral defines expected values for continuous densities, $\mathbb{E}[X] = \int x f(x)\,dx$, but fails for pathological cases like the indicator of the rationals. The Lebesgue integral, built on measure theory, resolves these limitations and is the foundation of rigorous probability theory in this topic.

Modes of convergence in probability (almost-sure, in probability, in distribution, $L^p$) generalize the sequence-convergence concepts of formalcalculus to random-variable sequences. The implications between modes — and the counterexamples that separate them — all sit on the $\varepsilon$–$N$ scaffolding.

The Borel–Cantelli lemmas — if $\sum P(A_n) < \infty$ then $P(\limsup A_n) = 0$ — are direct applications of series convergence to probability. Countable additivity of measures is itself defined via convergent series of set measures.

The divergence theorem yields Stein's identity $\mathbb{E}[\nabla \cdot F(X)] = -\mathbb{E}[F(X) \cdot \nabla \log p(X)]$ for a smooth density $p$ with suitable boundary conditions — the foundation of Stein-variational gradient descent and kernel Stein discrepancy.

Modes of convergence in probability extend the pointwise-vs-uniform distinction from deterministic function sequences to sequences of random variables. Uniform integrability — the probabilistic analog of equicontinuity — controls the interchange of limits and expectations in convergence proofs.

The $\sigma$-algebra and probability-measure axioms developed in the formalstatistics sample-spaces topic generalize, in measure-theoretic probability, to abstract measure spaces. The Kolmogorov axioms are the probability-specialization of the Lebesgue measure axioms, and this topic is where that generalization is made precise.

MAML's outer-loop meta-gradient is a Jacobian-of-a-Jacobian — the chain rule applied through the unrolled inner-loop SGD trajectory (equations 2.4–2.6). The Pearlmutter (1994) Hessian-vector-product identity (2.7) is a direct calculation in the calculus of vector-valued functions developed there.

Implicit MAML (Rajeswaran et al. 2019) bypasses recursive autograd by inverting the inner-loop fixed-point via the implicit function theorem. The IFT-based meta-gradient computation in §3.5 — equation (3.8) — is built on this calculus.

Meta-learning is the ML reading of hierarchical Bayes: tasks play the role of groups, MAML's θ₀ plays the role of group-level hyperparameters, and bilevel meta-optimization is the ML reading of §28's hierarchical MLE with group-level shrinkage. The present topic explicitly discharges the §28.10 Ex 14 forward-pointer to meta-learning.

Empirical Bayes — estimating the prior from data rather than fixing it a priori — is the conceptual ancestor of meta-optimization. Meta-learning generalizes the EB prior-estimation idea from data-within-a-task to tasks-within-a-distribution, as §6.3 makes precise.

Neural Processes sit at the boundary: parametric in the network weights but nonparametric in the implicit stochastic process they sample from. The §4 development cites this distinction without re-deriving it; the trained encoder–decoder pair amortizes a posterior over a function-space prior.

MDL codes data as parameter + residual; under exponential-family sufficiency, the optimal parameter code uses exactly the sufficient statistic, making MDL and sufficiency operationally equivalent in that setting. The data-processing inequality on the sufficient statistic is what justifies the two-part-code minimum-description-length objective.

The structural backbone of the entire topic. §1's three-pooling-regimes geometry, §3's BLUP shrinkage formula, and §5's frequentist–Bayesian bridge all assume the reader has internalized the partial-pooling theory developed there — the Stein-style shrinkage, the hierarchical model class, the James–Stein admissibility result that explains why shrinkage estimators dominate unbiased ones in sum-of-squares risk.

§2.4's GLS-as-BLUE / Aitken's theorem builds on the OLS / Gauss–Markov machinery developed there. The proof we sketch reduces GLS to OLS on a whitened system, which presupposes the standard OLS result that whitening preserves BLUE — proved in linear-regression as a consequence of the Gauss–Markov theorem.

§4.1's discussion of the ML downward bias for variance components is the application here of the general MLE small-sample bias theory developed there. The N-vs-(N-p) degrees-of-freedom correction is the prototype, and the §4.2 REML correction is the mixed-effects generalization.

The conditional-Gaussian identity used in §3 to derive the BLUP-as-posterior-mean reading — Cov(u, y) Cov(y)^-1 (y - E[y]) — is the standard multivariate-Normal conditioning formula, taught there in pure-probability form. The §2 marginal-distribution theorem also reduces to a standard MVN result via affine transformations.

§5.1's prior choices are weakly-informative priors per Gelman 2006, and the prior–likelihood–posterior decomposition of §5's PyMC fit relies on the Bayesian framework developed there. The flat-improper-prior marginalization in §4.2's REML derivation is also the simplest case of the improper-prior theory it covers.

Most of this topic is linear-Gaussian, so generalized-linear-models is best read as a related extension rather than a strict prerequisite. It becomes directly relevant in §6.2, where the discussion broadens from linear mixed models to GLMMs — the fixed-effects side inherits the link-function and exponential-family machinery developed there, and the marginal-likelihood factorization (4.2) generalizes but no longer factors closed-form.

The Bernoulli-with-logit and Poisson / Negative-Binomial-with-log-link GLMs covered in §6.2 build directly on the discrete distributions cataloged there. Mixed-effects extends those fixed-effects GLMs to the random-effects framework via the marginal-likelihood factorization developed in §4 — the random-intercepts logistic and Poisson regressions that the §6.2 GLMM discussion makes operational.

The Normal-response linear regression case (identity link) is the §2–§3 substrate developed in full via the V = ZGZᵀ + R marginal covariance and the BLUP shrinkage formula; Gamma-with-log-link GLMs (for positive-valued outcomes) appear in §6.2 as part of the GLMM extension to non-Gaussian likelihoods. Both build directly on the continuous distributions cataloged there.

§6.2's GLMM machinery — link function, IRLS-style fitting, deviance — assumes the response distribution lies in the exponential family. The canonical link function is (A')⁻¹ from the natural parameterization, and the exponential-family structure is what makes the marginal-likelihood factorization (4.2) closed-form in the linear-Gaussian case and tractable-via-Laplace in the GLMM extension.

The §6.2 Dirichlet–multinomial conjugate-update integral over the (K−1)-simplex and the §3.2 Bayes-error computation as an integral over the decision-region boundary are both standard multivariate-integration moves. The §4.3 normalization constant of the multivariate Gaussian also appears here, with the same use as in kernel-regression §6.

MLE first-order conditions in §4.2 (Gaussian NB), §5.2 (Multinomial NB), and §5.3 (Bernoulli NB) — set the log-likelihood gradient to zero and solve in closed form. The §7.2–7.3 Ng–Jordan asymptotic-rate proofs use Taylor-expansion machinery similar in spirit to kernel-regression's §3 bias derivation.

The Bernoulli / Multinomial / Categorical families that supply the class-conditional likelihoods in §5 (Multinomial NB, Bernoulli NB) and the Dirichlet conjugate prior in §6 are developed there. The discrete-distributions topic already declares formalmlConnections → naive-bayes for the Bernoulli-NB special case; this prereq closes the reciprocal and discharges the deferred-reciprocals.md entry.

The §6 derivation of Laplace add-one smoothing as a uniform Dirichlet prior, and the more general add-α smoothing as Dirichlet(α,...,α), draws directly on the conjugate-prior framework. The Dirichlet–multinomial conjugate pair developed there is what makes the posterior-predictive plug-in in §6.4 closed-form.

MLE for the per-class Gaussian mean and variance in §4.2, per-class token probabilities in §5.2, and per-class Bernoulli rates in §5.3 are all standard one-parameter-family MLE arguments. The §7.2 logistic-regression asymptotic-error bound also uses MLE asymptotics (Fisher information, asymptotic normality) as background.

Gaussian, multinomial, and Bernoulli are all exponential-family distributions; the linear-in-features log-posterior derived in §2.2 (and used implicitly through the topic) is the natural-parameter linearization that makes NB log-linear in the sufficient statistics. The §7 Ng–Jordan setup uses the exponential-family / GLM parameterization to align GNB and logistic regression on a shared model class.

The §4 Gaussian Naive Bayes derivation uses the multivariate Gaussian density and the diagonal-covariance assumption. The §4.4 LDA / QDA / GNB three-way comparison draws on multivariate-Gaussian decision-theory machinery (shared vs class-specific covariances, the quadric decision boundary). The §10.3 correlated-features failure mode also depends on multivariate-Gaussian intuition.

Naive Bayes and logistic regression are the canonical generative-discriminative pair of binary classifiers. Both fit within the GLM framework (logit link, exponential-family response), but they differ in how they fit the parameters (joint-density MLE vs conditional-likelihood MLE). The §7 Ng–Jordan asymptotic comparison is the cleanest illustration of when each parameterization wins. A future GLM revision in formalstatistics could naturally point back at this topic for the generative-side treatment.

The substitution rule for densities under a diffeomorphism — every flow's log-density formula in this topic is downstream of $p_X(x) = p_Z(T^{-1}(x)) \cdot |\det \partial T^{-1}/\partial x|$. We derive the $d$-dimensional version in §2.2 by taking the substitution rule as a load-bearing tool from formalcalculus.

The Jacobian determinant as the local volume-distortion factor, and the architectural design pressure for triangular Jacobians (coupling layers in §4, autoregressive flows in §5). Flows engineer their Jacobian structure to make $\log|\det \partial T/\partial z|$ computable in $O(d)$ time instead of $O(d^3)$.

Measure-theoretic foundation for densities, pushforwards, and the absolute-continuity hypothesis that makes the change-of-variables formula meaningful. We use the framework implicitly: the pushforward of an absolutely continuous measure under a diffeomorphism is again absolutely continuous, and its density is given by the Jacobian-determinant formula of §2.2.

The inverse-function theorem underpins the local-invertibility argument that justifies parameterizing flows by their forward direction: if $\det \partial T/\partial z > 0$ everywhere, $T$ is locally a diffeomorphism with smooth inverse, and the algebraic invertibility of the layer parameterization (§4.5) extends this to global invertibility.

Nonparametric density estimation by averaging kernel functions at training points; flows are the neural-parametric heir to this classical method. §10.2 contrasts the two: KDE's minimax rate degrades polynomially with dimension (the curse), while flows achieve parametric $O(n^{-1/2})$ at the cost of model-misspecification bias when the target lies outside the representable class.

The training objective in §7 is plain MLE applied to a flow's parametric family. Consistency, asymptotic efficiency, the bias-variance trade-off, and the consistency-under-regularity-conditions theorem all inherit directly from classical MLE theory; flows are just a particular choice of parametric family that supports closed-form gradient computation.

Standard multivariate Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ as the base distribution, the multivariate change-of-variables for the pushforward, and the joint / marginal / conditional decomposition used in the autoregressive form (§5). Multivariate Gaussian theory underlies almost every step of the flow framework.

Foundational framework for continuous random variables, distributions, and densities. Flows model continuous random variables $X$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ as deterministic transformations $X = T_\phi(Z)$ of a base random variable $Z \sim p_Z$; the basic theory of $X$, $Z$, and their densities is taken from this prerequisite.

Catalog of continuous probability distributions (Gaussian, mixtures, Student-$t$, and so on) along with their densities and standard properties. Each trained flow $p_\phi$ defines a continuous distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ whose density we evaluate via §2's change-of-variables formula; the §1 trichotomy and §10's KDE/GMM contrasts position flows within this catalog.

The Radon–Nikodym derivative dQ/dP — the central object of the change-of-measure inequality (§3) — requires the Lebesgue integral to define and the change-of-variables formula to manipulate. PAC-Bayes uses dQ/dP as the bridge between P-expectations and Q-expectations throughout §§3–6. Every appearance of E_Q[·] = ∫ · dQ in the proofs is a Lebesgue integral against the posterior measure.

The Donsker–Varadhan variational form of KL divergence (§3.3 Theorem 1) depends on the existence of the Radon–Nikodym derivative dQ/dP whenever Q is absolutely continuous w.r.t. P. This is the technical condition that makes the master tool of §3 well-defined, and consequently every PAC-Bayes bound presumes Q ≪ P from §2.3 onward.

Reciprocates an existing forward-pointer from formalStatistics §32, which declares PAC-Bayes as the posterior-averaged refinement of its function-class complexity arguments. PAC-Bayes inherits the empirical-process viewpoint — uniform deviations of empirical means from population means over function classes — and replaces the supremum over H with an expectation under Q, charging the drift KL(Q ∥ P) instead of the function-class complexity.

Maurer's 2004 moment lemma (§4.2 Lemma 1) and the Cramér-transform machinery underlying §4's MGF-based bound chain are the canonical large-deviations tools. PAC-Bayes is a posterior-averaged refinement of Cramér's theorem — the Donsker–Varadhan variational form of §3 IS the Legendre transform of relative entropy on the function space of bounded measurable functions.

KL divergence is an expected log-density-ratio (§3.1), and the moment generating function of the empirical risk is the technical workhorse of every bound proof in §§4–6. Both depend on the expectation-and-moments machinery developed there — in particular Hoeffding's MGF bound for bounded random variables, used directly in §6's Catoni proof.

The √(1/n) rate that all PAC-Bayes bounds achieve in the agnostic regime is the standard rate of convergence in probability for sample means of bounded random variables — the canonical statement of modes-of-convergence at the rate the kl-form and McAllester forms recover. The §7 fast-rate refinements give O(1/n) under low-variance conditions, which is the L²-convergence regime.

Universal-approximation theorems for neural networks (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991) are the neural-network analog of Weierstrass — networks form an algebra that separates points and approximates continuous functions densely. Barron's $O(1/\sqrt n)$ approximation rate, identical to Bernstein polynomials, gives the function-class boundedness on which PAC bounds operate.

The uniform-boundedness principle is the functional-analytic backbone of uniform convergence over function classes. Generalization bounds in this topic require function-class boundedness — a UBP consequence — to translate pointwise concentration into uniform statements over the hypothesis class $\mathcal H$.

Continuous hypothesis classes and the uniform convergence of empirical risk $\hat R_n(h) \to R(h)$ rely on continuity and compactness arguments developed in the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ framework. The Glivenko–Cantelli theorem is uniform continuity of the empirical CDF lifted to function classes.

Fourier analysis on Boolean functions $\{-1, 1\}^n$ uses Fourier coefficients $\hat f(S) = \mathbb{E}[f(x)\chi_S(x)]$, the discrete analog of the continuous Fourier coefficients. The KKL inequality and noise-sensitivity bounds — load-bearing tools for learnability on the Boolean cube — are Fourier-analytic results.

The convergence $\hat R_n(h) \to R(h)$ as $n \to \infty$ is a sequence-convergence result that we want to hold uniformly over the hypothesis class. The Glivenko–Cantelli theorem extends pointwise sequence convergence to uniform convergence over function classes — exactly the regime PAC bounds quantify.

The union bound converts uniform convergence over a hypothesis class into a series $\sum_h P(\text{bad event for } h)$. Finite VC dimension ensures this series is controlled (via Sauer–Shelah growth function), yielding the polynomial-in-$n$ generalization bounds that make PAC learning quantitative.

PAC learning is fundamentally a uniform-convergence theorem: $\hat R_n(h) \to R(h)$ uniformly over $h \in \mathcal H$ as $n$ grows, with the VC dimension quantifying the complexity of $\mathcal H$ and controlling the rate. Larger VC dimension means slower uniform convergence and a higher sample-complexity bound.

Topic 8's multivariate-Normal geometry — covariance matrix, marginal/conditional rules, the MVN density form — is the population-distribution substrate PCA estimates from samples. The spectral decomposition $\boldsymbol\Sigma = \mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf{Q}^\top$ developed there directly motivates the principal-directions / explained-variances picture; Theorem 7 (in fs) provides the MVN-specific connection to maximum-variance projection.

The formal foundation for both HL-style test-inversion (§4) and the conformal-quantile threshold (§2.3). The duality between a level-$\alpha$ test and a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence region is the abstract machinery behind every interval construction in this topic.

Split-conformal's quantile of conformity scores (Definition 7), QR's empirical conditional-quantile estimator (§3), and HL's Walsh-average ordering (§4) all rest on order-statistic theory. The asymptotic theory of empirical quantiles underlies the stability argument in Theorem 5.1 and the HL/conformal equivalence in Theorem 5.3.

The asymptotic alternative to finite-sample exchangeability arguments. The bootstrap discussion in §7.1 leans on Edgeworth expansions, the QR asymptotics cited in §3.3 use empirical-process limit theorems, and Theorem 5.1's proof appeals to uniform stability of empirical-quantile order statistics.

Self-contained treatment of the bootstrap principle, percentile and BCa intervals, and the conditions under which bootstrap-percentile intervals are valid — the third resampling-based interval-construction method, contrasted with conformal/CQR/HL in §7.1 of this topic.

§3.1's change-of-variables theorem for densities (Theorem 2) is a direct application of the multivariable change-of-variables formula for integrals. The Jacobian determinant calculation and the substitution argument used in the proof are taught there in pure-calculus form.

§3 computes Jacobians for the log, logit, and stick-breaking transforms throughout. The Jacobian-as-linearization view and the determinant interpretation as local volume scaling — both essential for understanding why the Jacobian factor appears in (3.1) — are the substrate developed in that topic.

§1.1's conjugate Beta-Binomial computation and §5.1's hierarchical prior specification both lean on the prior–likelihood–posterior decomposition that bayesian-foundations-and-prior-selection develops in detail. PP automates the posterior computation that topic does by hand.

§4.2 sketches NUTS operationally and defers convergence theory and detailed-balance proofs to bayesian-computation-and-mcmc. The leapfrog integrator, dual-averaging step-size adaptation, and divergent-transition concept used in §5.2's funnel diagnosis are all developed there.

§5's eight-schools example IS a hierarchical model with partial pooling. The hierarchical-bayes-and-partial-pooling topic develops the partial-pooling theory — when the hierarchical structure improves estimates over no-pooling and complete-pooling alternatives, and how partial pooling shrinks group-level estimates toward the hyperprior mean.

Proximal operators minimize $f(y) + (1/2t)\|y - x\|^2$, which is the second-order Taylor model of $f$ at $x$ plus a quadratic proximal penalty. The Moreau envelope uses the same Taylor-inspired local quadratic structure, and the descent-lemma analysis of forward-backward splitting borrows directly from the formalcalculus Taylor-with-remainder framework.

The OLS analog. Theorem 3's asymptotic normality of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta(\tau) - \beta(\tau)) \Rightarrow N(0, \tau(1-\tau)\, D^{-1} \Omega D^{-1})$ is the QR replacement of OLS's $\sqrt{n}(\hat\beta_{OLS} - \beta) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1})$. The Bernoulli factor $\tau(1-\tau)$ plays the role of $\sigma^2$; the density-weighted Gram matrix $D(\tau)$ sandwich-replaces $(X'X)^{-1}$. Reading linear-regression first makes the structural parallel transparent.

The no-covariate special case. With a single intercept feature, the KB78 estimator reduces to the empirical $\tau$-quantile of $\{Y_i\}$; Theorem 1 reduces to the classical pinball-loss minimization characterization (Topic 29 §29.4); Theorem 3 reduces to the standard Bahadur–Ghosh asymptotics (Topic 29 §29.6). Topic 29 §29.10 Remark 19 explicitly motivates QR as the covariate-conditional extension.

Theorem 3's full proof runs through Knight 1998's algebraic identity plus an empirical-process limit of the rescaled QR objective; the argmin lemma is the continuous-mapping step. Theorem 4's restricted-eigenvalue argument and oracle inequality both use empirical-process tools (covering numbers, self-normalized concentration). Topic 32 §32.5 covers the full scaffold.

Quantile regression minimises the check loss $\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - \mathbb{1}\{u < 0\})$; its $\psi$ is non-smooth but falls within the general M-estimation framework (modulo regularity). The scalar-intercept case is Topic 29 §29.4 / §29.6; quantile regression is the covariate-conditional extension. The mutual-relevance link is M-estimation framing — neither side is a strict prerequisite for the other.

The convergence theory of numerical ODE schemes — consistency, stability, and the Lax equivalence theorem — provides the analytical framework for understanding when discrete random walks approximate continuous diffusions, and at what rate. Brownian motion as the continuum limit of random walks (Donsker's invariance principle) is exactly such a Lax-style convergence statement.

MCMC sampling produces a sequence of states whose convergence to the target distribution is characterized by the mixing time — how many steps until the sequence is 'close enough' in total-variation distance. The convergence-rate analysis we do in §4 uses exactly the $\varepsilon$–$N$ machinery developed in formalcalculus.

Provides the H₀/H₁ framework, type-I error, $p$-value definition, and level-vs-size distinction that every section of this topic deploys without redefinition. The permutation-test exactness theorem in §2 is a finite-sample analog of the level-α framework developed there; the worked-example structure of §1 mirrors the same setup.

Ranks are a deterministic function of order statistics — $R_i$ is essentially the inverse of the order-statistic indexing. §3's Mann-Whitney variance derivation uses joint probabilities of order statistics; §6's Hodges-Lehmann CI inverts a rank statistic into a confidence interval expressible directly in terms of Walsh-average order statistics.

Required for the asymptotic null distributions throughout: the normal approximation to $W^+$ in §1, $U$ in §3, and the multivariate finite-population CLT (Hájek 1960) that powers §4's chi-squared limit. §5's Pitman ARE proof leans on the joint CLT under contiguous local alternatives plus Hoeffding's U-statistic CLT for the off-diagonal sum.

The Neyman-Pearson optimal test under correctly-specified parametric models — i.e., the $t$-test under normality — is the parametric foil against which §5's ARE compares Wilcoxon. The ARE framework asks: how much power do we lose by giving up the parametric optimum to gain distribution-freeness? The 0.955 figure says: very little under normality.

§6's Hodges-Lehmann distribution-free CI is the test-inversion construction applied to the Wilcoxon test, and Theorem 10's proof is a worked instance of the duality machinery developed there. The set-theoretic inversion 'a level-α test inverts to a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence region' is the load-bearing step in proving exact coverage.

Bootstrap and permutation are both resampling-based approaches to inference but differ in their null-hypothesis treatment. Bootstrap resamples with replacement under the empirical distribution (no symmetry assumption); permutation resamples without replacement under exchangeability (a stronger but more rewarding assumption). §7 contrasts the two explicitly when discussing rank-vs-raw statistics.

The §4.4 reparametrization trick is the canonical example of pathwise-derivative gradient computation: writing z = T_φ(ε, x) as a deterministic function of fixed-distribution noise ε lets the chain rule pass through the sampling step. The §5 InfoNCE loss backpropagation through the softmax also relies on standard multivariable derivatives. The §3.2 linear-AE gradient descent loop uses the matrix-derivative form of the squared-error loss.

The §4 marginal-likelihood integral p_θ(x) = ∫ p_θ(x|z) p(z) dz is a multivariate integral over a latent space of dimension d. The §3.4 Tweedie identity proof differentiates this convolution integral under the integral sign — a standard multiple-integral move whose rigorous justification requires the dominated-convergence theorem from this prereq topic.

§2 is built directly on the Fisher–Neyman factorization, Lehmann–Schefé minimality, and the Bayes-risk equivalence theorem developed in formalstatistics. The MLE framing is also what makes the §4.5 β-VAE objective interpretable as a Lagrangian relaxation of the variational MLE problem.

The KL divergence is the central information-theoretic quantity in §4 (ELBO regularization term D_KL(q_φ || p)), §5 (mutual information as KL between joint and product distributions), and §7 (the IB Lagrangian's relationship to KL projections via the Donsker–Varadhan representation). The closed-form Gaussian-vs-Gaussian KL of §4.3 is the explicit case we work with end-to-end.

The §3.2 Baldi–Hornik proof uses the spectral decomposition of the multivariate covariance matrix, the Ky Fan trace-maximization principle, and the orthogonal-projector characterization of the top-d eigenspace — all standard multivariate-distributions machinery. The Jacobian determinant of the auxiliary-variable bijection T_m is the unit-conversion factor that makes the trans-dim acceptance ratio dimensionally consistent across fibers of different dimensions. §§5 through 8 use this throughout, with the master acceptance ratio in §7 absorbing |det J_T| as the new ingredient versus fixed-dim MH.
